stimuli.text: Researchers want to investigate whether a new fertilizer increases tomato yield. They have 40 garden plots available.

Random samples of 15 were taken from two groups. The values of daily steps (thousands) are:

**Group 1:** 10, 12, 12, 15, 15, 16, 19, 21, 23, 26, 26, 28, 29, 29, 29

**Group 2:** 14, 14, 19, 22, 24, 27, 28, 28, 29, 32, 35, 39, 45, 45, 63
A school district claims that 30% of its students take public transit to school. A reporter suspects the true proportion is lower. In a random sample of 360 students, 97 take public transit.

Data were collected on hours studied per week (x) and exam score (y) for a sample of students. A scatterplot shows a linear pattern, and the residual plot shows no pattern. Computer output for the least-squares regression is shown.

```text
Predictor   Coef      SE Coef
Constant    35.8
x           3.5
S = 4.9    R-Sq = 71.0%
```

questions.stem: If the sample size quadruples, what happens to the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄?

options.why: Larger samples reduce variability.
It depends on n.
Correct. σ/√n: √4 = 2.

options.text: It is cut to one quarter
options.why: It depends on √n.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for p is (0.42, 0.51). Which claim is supported?

options.text: It is plausible that fewer than half the population has the trait
options.why: Correct. Values below 0.5 lie in the interval.

options.text: The population proportion must be greater than 0.5
options.why: Most of the interval is below 0.5.

options.text: Exactly 46.5% of the population has the trait
options.why: The center is an estimate.

options.text: There is a 95% probability that p is between 0.42 and 0.51
options.why: The probability statement applies to the method, not this interval.

questions.explanation: Values below 0.5 lie in the interval.

questions.stem: For a distribution of household incomes in a city, the mean is 39 and the median is 47. Which is the most likely shape?

options.why: In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are close.
The mean is pulled toward the tail.
A uniform distribution is symmetric, with mean near the median.
Correct. A long left tail pulls the mean below the median.

questions.explanation: Mean 39 < median 47: the mean is pulled toward the left tail.

questions.stem: A factory tests H₀: the defect rate is 2% versus Hₐ: it is greater than 2%. What is a Type I error in this context?

options.why: That is a sampling problem.

options.text: Correctly finding that the rate is higher
options.why: That is a correct decision.

options.text: Concluding the defect rate is 2% when it is actually higher
options.why: That is a Type II error.

options.text: Concluding the defect rate is greater than 2% when it actually is 2%
options.why: Correct. Rejecting a true H₀.

questions.stem: Why is the t distribution used instead of the normal distribution for inference about a mean?

options.text: Because t is used only for proportions
options.why: It is used for means.

options.text: Because the sample is always biased
options.why: Bias is unrelated.

options.text: Because sample means are never normal
options.why: They often are approximately normal.

options.text: Because σ is estimated by s, which adds variability
options.why: Correct. t has heavier tails to account for it.

questions.explanation: t has heavier tails to account for it.

questions.stem: Two independent random samples have n₁ = 32, s₁ = 19 and n₂ = 34, s₂ = 8. What is the standard error of x̄₁ − x̄₂?

options.why: Correct. √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).
Each sample contributes s²/n.
Add variances, then take the square root; standard errors do not add.
Variances add, even for a difference.

questions.stem: The data are: 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 22, 23, 23, 25, 35, 67. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which statement is correct?

options.text: Q1 = 12.5, Q3 = 24; values above 35.5 are outliers, so 67 is an outlier
options.why: The fence uses 1.5 × IQR, not 1 × IQR.

options.text: Q1 = 12.5, Q3 = 24; values above 41.3 are outliers, so 67 is an outlier
options.why: Correct. IQR = 11.5; upper fence = Q3 + 1.5·IQR = 41.3.

options.text: There are no outliers because every value is within 2 standard deviations of the mean
options.why: The 1.5 × IQR rule is the method asked for.

options.text: Q1 = 12.5, Q3 = 24; values above 33.3 are outliers
options.why: Add 1.5·IQR to Q3, not to the median.

questions.stem: Each of 10 independent trials succeeds with probability 0.7. What is the probability of at most 4 successes?

options.why: That is only P(X = k).
Correct. Use the binomial distribution with n = 10 and p = 0.7.
That is P(X < k); 'at most k' includes k.
That is the complement.

questions.stem: The correlation between hours studied and exam score is r = 0.8. Which is a correct interpretation of r²?

options.text: About 64% of the predictions are correct
options.why: r² is about variation explained, not accuracy of individual predictions.

options.text: Hours studied causes 64% of exam score
options.why: Regression does not establish causation.

options.text: About 80% of the variation in exam score is accounted for by the model
options.why: Square r.

options.text: About 64% of the variation in exam score is accounted for by the linear model relating exam score to hours studied
options.why: Correct. r² is the proportion of variation in y explained by the linear model.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for μ₁ − μ₂ is (−2.4, 5.1). What can be concluded?

options.text: There is no convincing evidence of a difference in population means, because 0 is in the interval
options.why: Correct. Zero is a plausible difference.
Negative differences are also plausible.
Positive differences are also plausible.

options.text: The two means are exactly equal
options.why: The interval does not prove equality.

questions.stem: A radio station asks listeners to call in with their opinions about a new law. Which type of bias is most likely?

options.why: The question wording is not the main issue.

options.text: No bias, because listeners chose freely
options.why: Self-selection causes bias.
Correct. People with strong opinions are more likely to call.
The main problem is self-selection.

questions.explanation: People with strong opinions are more likely to call.

questions.stem: The regression line is ŷ = 22 + 1.9x. An observation has x = 20 and y = 54. What is its residual, and what does it mean?

options.text: 6; the actual value is above the predicted value
options.why: Residual = actual − predicted, not predicted − actual.
That is the predicted value ŷ.

options.text: -6; the actual value is below the predicted value
options.why: Correct. Residual = y − ŷ.

options.text: -6; the actual value is above the predicted value
options.why: A positive residual means the point is above the line.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 360 adults in a city, 245 use public transit weekly. Which is a 90% confidence interval for the proportion of all adults in a city who use public transit weekly?

options.why: Use the standard error, √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
Correct. p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) with z* = 1.645.
Use z* for 90%, not 1.96.
Divide by n inside the square root.

questions.stem: A variable is approximately normal with mean 110 and standard deviation 20. What proportion of values are greater than 98?

options.why: That is the other side of the boundary.
Divide by σ when standardizing.
Use the normal distribution's area, not the z-score.

questions.stem: Researchers recruited 200 volunteers among customers of the store and asked which of two study apps they already use, then compared test scores. Can the researchers conclude that the app causes higher scores, and to whom do the results apply?

options.text: No to cause and effect, and no generalization beyond the volunteers
options.why: Correct. No random assignment decides causation; no random selection decides generalization.

options.text: Yes to cause and effect, and yes to generalizing to all customers of the store
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

options.text: Yes to cause and effect, but only for the volunteers in the study
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

options.text: No to cause and effect, but the association can be generalized to all customers of the store
options.why: Random assignment allows causal conclusions; random selection allows generalization to the population.

questions.explanation: Random assignment: no. Random selection: no.

questions.stem: A student is chosen at random from those who drive to school. What is the probability the student is a junior?

options.why: Correct. P(junior | drives) = juniors who drive ÷ all who drive.
That is P(junior) overall.
That is P(drives | junior).
That is P(junior and drives); divide by drivers only.

questions.stem: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A and B) = 0.24. What is P(A or B), and are A and B independent?

options.why: Correct. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); independent if P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.24.
Compare P(A and B) with P(A)·P(B) = 0.24.
P(A and B) is not 0, so they are not mutually exclusive.
Subtract P(A and B) so the overlap is not counted twice.

questions.stem: Each of 10 independent devices fails with probability 0.02. What is the probability that at least one fails?

options.why: That is the probability all fail.
That is the probability none fail.
Correct. 1 − P(none fail) = 1 − (1 − p)^n.
Probabilities of overlapping events cannot simply be added.

questions.stem: The slope of a regression line predicting exam score from hours studied is 3.5. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Each student's score increases by exactly 3.5 points per hour
options.why: The slope describes predicted, not actual, values.

options.text: 35% of the variation in scores is explained
options.why: That is r².

options.text: A student who studies 0 hours scores 3.5
options.why: That would be the intercept.

options.text: For each additional hour studied, the predicted exam score increases by about 3.5 points
options.why: Correct. Slope is the predicted change in y per unit of x.

questions.explanation: Slope is the predicted change in y per unit of x.

questions.stem: Which graph is appropriate for displaying the distribution of favorite music genres among students?

options.why: Boxplots are for quantitative data.
Correct. Genre is categorical.
Scatterplots need two quantitative variables.
Histograms are for quantitative data.

The alternative is one-sided.

options.why: Weight each value by its probability.
That is the largest probability, not the mean.
That is the most likely value (mode), not the mean.

questions.stem: What does '95% confident' mean for a confidence interval?

options.text: 95% of samples will have the same p̂
options.why: Sample proportions vary.

options.text: 95% of the data fall within the interval
options.why: Intervals estimate a parameter, not the data's spread.

options.text: The parameter is in this interval with probability 0.95
options.why: The parameter is fixed; it is in or not.

options.text: In many repeated samples, about 95% of intervals built this way would capture the true parameter
options.why: Correct. Confidence describes the method's long-run success rate.

questions.explanation: Confidence describes the method's long-run success rate.

questions.stem: What is the smallest sample size needed to estimate a proportion with a margin of error of at most 0.05 at 99% confidence, with no prior estimate of p?

options.why: Always round up to guarantee the margin.
Multiply by p̂(1 − p̂) = 0.25.
Square z*/m.
Correct. n ≥ (z*/m)²(0.5)(0.5) with z* = 2.576, rounded up.

options.why: Correct. z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n); one-sided p-value.
The alternative is one-sided.
Find the area in the direction of Hₐ.

options.why: Correct. By the CLT, x̄ is approximately normal with SD 12/√100 = 1.2.
Use σ/√n for a sample mean.
Divide σ by √n, not n.
That is the area below.

options.why: Correct. Means add or subtract; variances add.
Standard deviations do not add; variances do.
Check the sign of the mean.
That is the variance; take the square root.

questions.stem: A random sample of 30 gives x̄ = 174.1 and s = 10. Test H₀: μ = 173 versus Hₐ: μ > 173. What are the test statistic and p-value?

options.why: The alternative is one-sided.
Divide by the standard error s/√n.
Correct. t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) with df = n − 1.
Use the t distribution, not the normal.

questions.stem: For a set of data, x̄ = 47, sx = 3, ȳ = 36, sy = 14 and r = 0.8. What is the least-squares regression line?

options.why: Multiply sy/sx by r.
a = ȳ − b·x̄.
Correct. b = r·sy/sx and a = ȳ − b·x̄.
The slope is r·sy/sx, not r·sx/sy.

questions.stem: Assuming the null hypothesis of a chi-square test is true, what is the expected count for Group 1, Option A?

options.why: That is the observed count.
Correct. Expected = (row total × column total) / table total.
Divide by the table total once.
Expected counts depend on the row and column totals.

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 118 of 200 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 146 of 270 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

options.why: Correct. Pooled p̂c = 0.5617; z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̂c(1 − p̂c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)).
The test uses the pooled proportion, because H₀ assumes p₁ = p₂.
Divide the difference by its standard error.
Use (1/n₁ + 1/n₂).

questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 23 of 80 subjects improved with treatment 1 and 59 of 120 improved with treatment 2. For a test of H₀: p₁ − p₂ = 0, what is the test statistic?

options.why: The test uses the pooled proportion, because H₀ assumes p₁ = p₂.
Use (1/n₁ + 1/n₂).
Divide the difference by its standard error.
Correct. Pooled p̂c = 0.41; z = (p̂₁ − p̂₂)/√(p̂c(1 − p̂c)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)).

parts.prompt: Write an investigative question for this study, and identify the explanatory and response variables.

rubric.criterion: A clear investigative question that names the population or units and the variables.
rubric.example: "Does the new fertilizer lead to a better total weight of tomatoes harvested than the standard fertilizer for units like these?"
Explanatory: treatment (the new fertilizer vs the standard fertilizer). Response: total weight of tomatoes harvested.

parts.prompt: Explain why an experiment, rather than an observational study, should be used to answer the question.

rubric.criterion: Only random assignment allows a cause-and-effect conclusion; an observational study could be confounded.
rubric.example: Units that choose a treatment may differ in other ways that affect the response.

parts.prompt: Describe how to randomly assign the 40 units to the two treatments in a completely randomized design.

rubric.example: Number units 1–40; use a random number generator to select 20 different numbers.
Those 20 receive the new fertilizer; the remaining 20 receive the standard fertilizer.

parts.prompt: The researchers consider blocking by sun exposure (full sun or partial shade). Explain how blocking would be carried out and why it could improve the experiment.

rubric.criterion: Form blocks and randomize within each block.
rubric.example: Separate units into the blocks, then randomly assign half of each block to each treatment.

rubric.criterion: Benefit: reduces variability in the response due to the blocking variable, making a treatment effect easier to detect.
rubric.example: Accounts for differences caused by sun exposure.

parts.prompt: Find the five-number summary for each group.
Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to determine whether Group 2 has any outliers. Show your work.

rubric.example: IQR = 17; upper fence = 39 + 1.5(17) = 64.5. No outliers.

parts.prompt: Compare the distributions of the two groups (shape, center and variability) in context.

rubric.example: The median for Group 2 (28) is greater than for Group 1 (21).
Group 2 is more variable (IQR 17 vs 13).

rubric.criterion: Comments on shape or unusual features.
rubric.example: Describes the shapes using the summaries.

parts.prompt: Which measure of center is more appropriate for Group 2, the mean or the median? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Median, because it is resistant to the outlier or skew.
rubric.example: Mean 30.9 is pulled toward the high value; median 28 is not.

parts.prompt: State the hypotheses, defining the parameter.

rubric.criterion: Correct hypotheses with the parameter defined.
rubric.example: H₀: p = 0.3; Hₐ: p < 0.3, where p is the proportion of all district students who take public transit.

parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate procedure and check its conditions.

rubric.criterion: One-sample z test for a proportion.
rubric.example: Random sample stated.
360 is less than 10% of all students (assumed); np₀ = 108 and n(1 − p₀) = 252 are both at least 10.

parts.prompt: Calculate the test statistic and p-value.
State a conclusion in context at α = 0.05.

rubric.criterion: Correct decision linked to the p-value, in context.
rubric.example: Because 0.1029 is greater than 0.05, fail to reject H₀: not convincing evidence that the proportion is less than 0.3.

parts.prompt: Write the equation of the least-squares regression line, defining the variables.

rubric.example: ŷ = 35.8 + 3.5x, where ŷ is predicted exam score and x is hours studied per week.

parts.prompt: Interpret the slope and the value of R-Sq in context.

rubric.example: For each additional unit of hours studied per week, the predicted exam score increases by about 3.5.
About 71.0% of the variation in exam score is accounted for by the linear model with hours studied per week.

parts.prompt: One observation has x = 11 and y = 72.1. Calculate and interpret its residual. Also find the correlation r.

rubric.example: ŷ = 74.3; residual = 72.1 − 74.3 = -2.2: the actual value is below the prediction.

parts.prompt: The data come from a convenience sample. Explain how this affects the conclusions and describe a better data collection method.

rubric.criterion: Results may not generalize to the population; a random sample would allow generalization.
rubric.example: Take a simple random sample of students from the population of interest. Observational data also cannot show causation.
